title: Dark nebula
description: Type of interstellar cloud that obscures visible light
wiki_lead:
A dark nebula or absorption nebula is a type of interstellar cloud, particularly molecular clouds, that is so dense that it obscures the visible wavelengths of light from objects behind it, such as background stars and emission or reflection nebulae. The extinction of the light is caused by interstellar dust grains in the coldest, densest parts of molecular clouds. Clusters and large complexes of dark nebulae are associated with Giant Molecular Clouds. Isolated small dark nebulae  are called Bok globules. Like other interstellar dust or material, the objects obscured are visible only using radio waves or infrared light, using techniques from radio and infrared astronomy
Dark clouds appear so because of sub-micrometre-sized dust particles, coated with frozen carbon monoxide and nitrogen, which effectively block the passage of light at visible wavelengths. Also present are molecular hydrogen, atomic helium, C18O (CO with oxygen as the 18O isotope), CS, NH3 (ammonia), H2CO (formaldehyde), c-C3H2 (cyclopropenylidene) and a molecular ion N2H+ (diazenylium), all of which are relatively transparent.
The form of such dark clouds is very irregular: they have no clearly defined outer boundaries and sometimes take on convoluted serpentine shapes. The closest and largest dark nebulae are visible to the naked eye, since they are the least obscured by stars in between Earth and the nebula, and because they have the largest angular size, appearing as dark patches against the brighter background of the Milky Way like the Coalsack Nebula and the Great Rift. These naked-eye objects are sometimes known as dark cloud constellations and take on a variety of names.
In the central regions of dark nebulae and molecular clouds, events such as the formation of stars and maser emission take place.

Complexes and constellations
Along with molecular clouds, dark nebulae make up molecular cloud complexes.
Dark nebulae form part of dark cloud constellations, recognisable in the night sky with the naked eye.
grok_lead: A dark nebula, also known as an absorption nebula, is an interstellar cloud of gas and dust so dense that it obscures visible light from stars and other bright objects behind it, appearing as a dark silhouette against the backdrop of the Milky Way or emission nebulae. These clouds are primarily composed of molecular hydrogen with a high concentration of dust grains, which absorb and scatter optical wavelengths, rendering them opaque at visible light but somewhat transparent in infrared. Typically cool, with temperatures ranging from 10 to 100 Kelvin, dark nebulae vary in size from small Bok globules (less than 3 light-years across and under 2,000 solar masses) to vast giant molecular clouds spanning over 200 parsecs and exceeding 1 million solar masses. Dark nebulae play a crucial role in stellar evolution as primary sites of star formation, where their low temperatures and relatively high densities allow the gas to collapse under its own gravity, eventually igniting new stars within the clouds. They are often observed as dark lanes or patches silhouetting brighter emission or reflection nebulae, such as the prominent Horsehead Nebula in the constellation Orion, a finger-like protrusion approximately 1,300 light-years away that blocks light from the IC 434 emission region. Other notable examples include the Coal Sack Nebula near the Southern Cross, visible to the naked eye in the Southern Hemisphere as a prominent dark area splitting the Milky Way's glow, and the Snake Nebula in Ophiuchus, an S-shaped feature requiring telescopic observation. Historically, these features were first systematically cataloged in 1919 by astronomer Edward Emerson Barnard, who identified 182 dark nebulae based on their obscuring effects. In modern astronomy, dark nebulae are studied using infrared telescopes to peer through their dust, revealing embedded protostars and molecular compositions that inform models of galaxy formation and the interstellar medium. Recent observations, such as those from the James Webb Space Telescope in 2024, have provided unprecedented details of structures within dark nebulae like the Horsehead.
